subtitle: Why do employees from underrepresented groups stay or leave? Explore workplace experiences and access to opportunity, without assuming that everyone in a group shares one reason for staying or leaving.
scope: For DHS leaders examining retention and employee experience. Use approved, appropriately protected information and responsible HR, equal-opportunity and data practices guidance. This course does not authorize identity-based employment preferences, informal personnel profiling, new retention periods, or changes to bargaining agreements. All cases and figures are practice.
introTranscript: Retention is not a promise that every employee will stay. People make career decisions for many reasons, and leaders cannot infer those reasons from identity or one survey answer. Leaders can examine the workplace conditions within their influence: clear expectations, fair access to development, respectful treatment, useful support and a credible response to concerns. This course connects listening with process evidence and practical action. It includes ways to interpret differences carefully, protect privacy and distinguish a retention initiative from the formal handling of an employment concern. Staff do their own work with consultant guidance when helpful; no mandatory consultant approval is created by these exercises.

lessons.title: Define the retention question before interpreting a pattern
lessons.summary: Specify the group, period and decision while keeping representation different from individual preference.
lessons.objective: Write a retention question with a defined population and period.
objectives: Write a retention question with a defined population and period.
Distinguish underrepresentation, turnover and employee experience as different questions.
Identify an unsupported explanation attached to a group difference.
takeaways: Define who and what the figures describe.
Representation is not a diagnosis of experience.
A difference raises a question before it explains a cause.
lessons.statement: A pattern can guide an investigation without telling you why a particular person left.

image.caption: A clear question keeps workforce figures connected to a decision.

intro.heading: Begin with the question the leader can act on
intro.body:
A leader may hear that a group is underrepresented and conclude that its members must have a particular retention problem. That conclusion combines several different questions. Representation describes the composition of a defined workforce compared with a relevant reference. Turnover describes departures during a period. Employee experience concerns what people encounter at work. These can be connected, but none should be used as an automatic explanation for the others.

Write the decision question before examining figures. For example: “What should we examine about access to development in this work unit over the last completed year?” Define the unit, period and eligible employees. Clarify whether a count includes all departures, only voluntary departures or movement to another state role. A person moving within the agency is not the same event as someone leaving state employment. Ask HR or the responsible data role to confirm definitions.

Use an appropriate reference rather than an arbitrary comparison. A small specialized team may not be comparable to the whole agency. A change in staffing, job mix or contract arrangement can affect figures. Do not publish identifiable small groups or invent a minimum reporting threshold; follow the responsible data guidance for the actual setting.

When a difference appears, state what is known and what is not. “The recorded departure rate differed during this period” is a description. “People from this group are not committed” is an unsupported judgment. A higher rate may justify examining opportunity, workload, climate or external factors, but the figure alone does not determine which explanation is correct.

The title of this course identifies a workforce equity concern, not a permission to treat individuals as representatives or to favor employees solely because of identity. Fair access and current employment requirements remain important. A disciplined question makes it easier to select a proportionate action based on relevant evidence.

lessons.keyStatement: Describe the pattern accurately before choosing an explanation or intervention.

flashcards.back: Continuing employment within a defined workplace or employment boundary over a specified period.
Departures measured with a stated definition and time period. Different definitions can produce different results.
A difference between workforce composition and an appropriate reference, examined with responsible guidance.
The population used to calculate a rate; it must match the question and the counted events.
A statement that one factor produced an outcome; a simple difference does not establish that claim.

items.title: Composition of the workforce
items.body: Ask what population and reference are appropriate and which positions are included. Composition can highlight an equity question but does not tell you what every employee experiences. Use current, authorized workforce information and responsible definitions rather than a leader’s impression of who belongs to a group.

items.title: Movement and departure
items.body: Clarify where people moved and what departure means. A promotion elsewhere in DHS, retirement and departure from state employment raise different questions. Do not combine events because a single figure is simpler to present. The definition should remain stable enough to make a comparison meaningful.

items.title: Experience within the workplace
items.body: Employees can remain while experiencing barriers, or leave for reasons unrelated to the unit. Listening and process evidence help examine the experience without making identity-based assumptions. Participation should not become a test of loyalty, and individual accounts should not be exposed in a public dashboard.

tabs.label: Boundary
tabs.body: The boundary defines what the figures describe: unit, roles, population and period. Departures from a small project group are not automatically comparable with departures across a whole agency. Explain inclusion and counting rules before interpreting the pattern. A clear boundary lets the reader understand both the possible concern and how far the evidence can reasonably travel.

tabs.label: Comparison
tabs.body: A comparison needs compatible definitions and context. A group with temporary appointments or a changing role mix may show different departures for several reasons. Work with the responsible data role to understand those differences. This does not dismiss a disparity; it prevents a reference figure from appearing to explain a workplace cause that it cannot establish.

tabs.label: Decision
tabs.body: The decision connects the inquiry to an arrangement a leader can examine, such as access to development or a confusing supervision route. Without that connection, a retention chart may become a label attached to people. Ask what additional evidence could inform a practical change while preserving privacy, formal authority and uncertainty about individual choices.

check.question: A small unit records more departures in one group during one quarter. What is justified first?
check.correct: Confirm definitions and privacy limits, describe the pattern cautiously and identify further evidence needed to examine possible explanations.
wrong: Declare that the group has low commitment.
Publish individual departure histories so readers can investigate.
Assume the pattern proves discrimination without further examination.
check.feedbackCorrect: This treats the figure as a question to investigate and preserves accuracy and appropriate data handling.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A departure pattern cannot establish low commitment or another personal motive. Publishing individual histories creates privacy risks and still does not explain a group-level cause. Declaring discrimination from one small quarterly difference exceeds the evidence. Confirm definitions and appropriate handling, describe the concern cautiously and examine relevant explanations through responsible review.

items.text: Recorded voluntary departures from the unit during a stated completed year.
The turnover figure includes unspecified kinds of movement.
The group leaves because its members do not value public service.
The workforce count includes identified roles at the stated point in time.
The reference population uses unknown job categories.
One quarter proves a single cause for every departure.

lessons.next: Next, listen to employee experience without assigning a shared story.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Samira sees three departures in a small role group and a slide calling this a retention crisis. Two employees moved to other DHS roles, and one retired. The slide does not identify its period or definition.
options: A clearer definition of the events, population and period, with appropriate data handling before interpreting the pattern.
A public list of the three employees and their identities.
An immediate conclusion that the unit’s culture caused all three departures.
responses: This makes the finding interpretable and separates different events before drawing an explanation.
Personal disclosure does not resolve the unclear definition and can create avoidable privacy risks.
The available facts do not establish one cause and include different kinds of movement.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice retention question and its population, period, departure definition and decision purpose. List two explanations the figures alone cannot establish.

move.control: You can define a decision question, request responsible definitions and describe evidence limits.
move.failure: A vague figure becomes a confident story about a group or an individual.
move.next: Before using a retention slide, check its definitions and what conclusion the underlying evidence supports.

lessons.title: Listen without assuming a shared experience
lessons.summary: Invite accounts of workplace arrangements while making participation useful, voluntary and appropriately private.
lessons.objective: Write an experience question that does not presume a group’s reason for leaving.
objectives: Write an experience question that does not presume a group’s reason for leaving.
Explain how input will be used and the limits of privacy.
Distinguish voluntary listening from the handling of a formal concern.
takeaways: Ask about experience, not presumed motives.
Explain the use and limits of input.
Formal concerns retain their responsible routes.
lessons.statement: People with a shared identity can have different experiences, needs and career decisions.

image.caption: Careful listening invites specific experiences without requiring personal disclosure.

intro.heading: Ask what happens in the work
intro.body:
Listening can help a leader understand what a workforce figure cannot show. It can also become burdensome when a leader asks employees to explain an entire group or repeatedly tell painful experiences without visible follow-through. A useful invitation identifies the workplace question, how the information may affect a decision and what the employee can choose to share. It should not imply that staying, leaving or participating demonstrates loyalty.

Ask about arrangements people encounter. “How do employees find out about development opportunities?” invites an account of a process. “Why does your group leave?” presumes a shared experience and makes the person a representative. Follow a broad question with a specific example, such as the last occasion the employee wanted useful feedback or access to a project. Do not require an identity disclosure to offer a process suggestion.

Offer appropriate ways to contribute, with current responsible guidance on privacy and records. A small focus group cannot promise anonymity merely because names are removed from a summary. Explain who receives the information and avoid collecting unnecessary details. Use approved channels for actual employee information; course exercises should use invented examples.

Listening is not the same as investigating a formal concern. If someone raises discrimination, accommodation, safety or another matter requiring a designated process, explain the appropriate route and the leader’s responsibilities. Do not promise to keep everything off the record, require informal mediation before a formal route, or use a general feedback session to make a personnel determination.

Return a useful response. Tell participants which process question will be examined, what can change and which request requires a different authority. Even a small improvement should show its relationship to the input. If nothing can change, explain the limitation honestly rather than continuing to request the same stories.

lessons.keyStatement: Listening becomes credible when people can see its purpose, boundaries and follow-through.

items.title: An assumed reason for leaving
items.body: Replace “why are people like you leaving?” with a question about workplace arrangements and experiences the employee chooses to describe. Leave space for a different answer or no answer. People may have several reasons, and they do not owe the supervisor a representative explanation.

items.title: A promise of complete anonymity
items.body: Check what can actually be protected and who may recognize an account. Describe the approved handling process rather than making a blanket promise. Small groups, distinctive events and role descriptions can reveal a person even without their name. Seek responsible data guidance before summarizing sensitive input.

items.title: A formal concern during a check-in
items.body: Listen respectfully, explain the responsible route and follow applicable duties. A stay conversation should not become a substitute investigation or a requirement to resolve the issue informally. Preserve access to formal processes while continuing appropriate practical support.

tabs.label: Invitation
tabs.body: An invitation tells employees which workplace arrangement is open to examination and how their input may matter. A voluntary stay conversation should not require a promise to remain. Explain the purpose and information handling accurately so participation is informed. Listening can identify a barrier, but it does not by itself authorize a formal remedy or guarantee retention.

tabs.label: Question
tabs.body: A question should invite a specific experience, such as difficulty discovering a project opportunity. Asking why a whole group leaves assumes shared motives and makes one employee answer for others. A concrete prompt allows different explanations and practical detail. Keep the conversation focused on the work rather than requiring private identity accounts or assigning commitment labels.

tabs.label: Response
tabs.body: A response closes the gap between listening and action. Explain what will be examined, who is responsible and what requires another role. An employee may still choose to leave; that does not erase an issue that needs attention. A modest documented next step is more credible than assuring the person that every concern will disappear if they stay.

check.question: Which question best supports a useful stay conversation?
check.correct: Which work arrangements help you contribute, and where have you had to work around a barrier you want us to examine?
wrong: Why do employees from your background leave our division?
Will you promise to stay if we hold this conversation?
Which coworker should we label as resistant to inclusion?
check.feedbackCorrect: This invites a concrete experience without requiring a shared group story or a commitment to remain.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Asking why a background group leaves makes one person speak for others and presumes a shared cause. A promise to stay turns listening into a loyalty test. Labeling a coworker resistant substitutes a personal judgment for a concrete work question. Invite a specific barrier or helpful arrangement and explain how the response may inform action.

items.text: Ask how employees learn about project opportunities.
Publish a quote from the only employee in a small role group.
Ask one employee to explain everyone with their background.
Explain which process decision the input may inform.
Promise anonymity without checking distinctive details.
Treat a group label as the reason for an employee’s answer.

lessons.next: Next, examine the opportunity and support processes behind the experience.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Tessa plans a stay conversation with Amari after hearing a concern about uneven access to assignments. Her draft asks Amari to explain why employees with his background leave and promises no one will ever know what he says.
options: Keep the draft because the promise will encourage honesty.
Ask about assignment access, explain approved handling and formal routes, and avoid making Amari represent a group.
Require an answer before considering Amari for another project.
responses: The question presumes a shared story, and the privacy promise may be impossible to keep.
This focuses on the process while preserving choice, accurate privacy expectations and formal support routes.
This would turn listening into an employment gate and undermine the purpose of the conversation.

lessons.transfer: Draft a listening invitation with a purpose, two process questions, an accurate use statement and a responsible route for formal concerns.

move.control: You can ask neutral questions, clarify handling and give a practical response without demanding personal disclosure.
move.failure: Employees are asked for sensitive stories, but cannot tell what will change or where formal support is available.
move.next: Revise the next listening invitation to show the decision purpose and follow-through owner.

lessons.title: Examine access to opportunity and support
lessons.summary: Trace the process from invitation to usable development rather than assuming equal announcements create equal access.
lessons.objective: Map the steps required to obtain one development opportunity.
objectives: Map the steps required to obtain one development opportunity.
Identify a barrier that arises before formal selection.
Propose a process improvement while preserving applicable employment rules.
takeaways: Access begins before a selection decision.
An invitation needs time and usable support.
lessons.statement: The same announcement does not guarantee that employees have a usable chance to participate.

image.caption: An opportunity becomes usable through clear information and practical support.

intro.heading: Follow the opportunity from start to finish
intro.body:
Leaders may describe development access as fair because an announcement went to everyone. The announcement is only one step. Employees must discover the opportunity, understand its purpose, believe they can ask about it, obtain the necessary approval, have time to participate and receive useful follow-through. A barrier at any point can make an apparently open opportunity difficult to use.

Map one actual process with responsible colleagues, without collecting unnecessary personnel information. How is a project role announced? Which criteria are explained? How is interest expressed? Who decides? What happens to normal workload? What support is provided and how is the experience recognized afterward? A map helps distinguish a selection concern from a workload or information concern.

Look for assumptions that favor familiarity. A supervisor may invite the person who was visible at a recent meeting, assume someone with caregiving responsibilities would decline, or treat an employee’s quiet communication style as a lack of ambition. Ask about interest and relevant capability rather than making the choice on the employee’s behalf. Actual assignments and promotions must follow current HR, bargaining and selection requirements.

Support matters as much as invitation. If an assignment adds hours without removing any work, employees with already heavy workloads may have little practical choice. If only participants with established contacts receive feedback, the opportunity may reproduce the same pattern. Clarify the learning purpose, authorized time and feedback responsibilities within the available authority.

A process improvement should address the identified barrier. A clearer interest route may be more useful than another broad message. A workload discussion may be necessary before participation. A formal promotion question needs HR guidance. Avoid promising outcomes based on identity or using a voluntary course as a new eligibility requirement. The goal is to make relevant opportunities and support explainable and usable.

lessons.keyStatement: Examine the whole opportunity path, including information, time, selection and follow-through.

items.title: Only familiar employees hear early
items.body: An opportunity can be formally announced after a favored person has already prepared. Check how information travels and when interest is invited. Improve visibility and explain criteria before decisions where the applicable process permits. Do not treat an informal early conversation as an authorized selection.

items.title: Participation adds work without support
items.body: An employee may want the opportunity and still lack a usable way to take it on. Discuss workload, time and responsible approvals. Avoid interpreting a declined assignment as low ambition until the arrangement is understood. A fair invitation includes a realistic account of the commitment.

items.title: A leader assumes someone would decline
items.body: Assumptions about age, family, disability or culture should not replace asking about interest through the appropriate process. The employee can describe their own priorities. Offer relevant information and explain the requirements without promising a selection result or demanding private justification.

tabs.label: Before the choice
tabs.body: Before the choice, examine whether employees could discover the opportunity, understand requirements and express interest in time. A message sent to everyone may still use unexplained terminology or an informal selection route. Review the actual path rather than interpreting nonparticipation as lack of ambition. Formal criteria and authorized decisions remain in effect.

tabs.label: During the work
tabs.body: During the work, support determines whether participation is practical. An employee carrying an unrevised workload may have an invitation but no usable time to develop. Confirm approved workload, access and feedback arrangements with responsible roles. More reminders will not repair a time barrier, and expecting invisible extra labor shifts the opportunity’s costs onto the employee.

tabs.label: After the work
tabs.body: After the work, examine what was learned and how contribution became visible. A useful analysis can demonstrate capability without guaranteeing promotion. Recognize the employee’s actual reasoning and result, explain possible next learning steps and preserve the applicable selection process. Otherwise a development invitation can become either empty praise or an outcome promise the leader cannot deliver.

check.question: A development announcement reaches everyone, but only employees with manageable workloads can participate. What should the leader examine?
check.correct: The workload and support arrangements as well as the invitation and selection process.
wrong: Whether employees who decline are insufficiently motivated.
Whether announcements can be made even more frequent without changing support.
Whether participation should automatically guarantee promotion.
check.feedbackCorrect: A usable opportunity depends on the complete process, including time and support within approved authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling employees unmotivated ignores whether participation is practical. More announcements do not create workable time or feedback. Automatic promotion confuses development access with a separate formal selection decision. Examine the invitation, criteria, approved workload and support so the opportunity can be used without invented outcomes or hidden extra labor.

items.text: Employees do not know how to express interest.
Project duties are added with no workload discussion.
A promotion must follow the applicable recruitment process.
Selection criteria are explained only after the choice.
Participants receive no agreed feedback or access to needed materials.
A proposed change affects classification or bargaining provisions.

lessons.next: Next, respond to workplace concerns without replacing formal processes.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Rafael finds that an open project role is repeatedly accepted by the same two employees. Others report that taking it would add evening work because no existing duties are adjusted. Rafael had assumed everyone else lacked ambition.
options: Praise only the two participants for commitment.
Make acceptance compulsory for the remaining employees.
Review authorized workload and support arrangements, clarify interest and criteria, and seek HR guidance where required.
responses: This turns unequal practical access into a personality judgment.
Compulsion does not create usable support and may conflict with the actual assignment process.
This examines the whole opportunity path and preserves the responsible authority for employment decisions.

lessons.transfer: Map a practice development opportunity from discovery through follow-up. Identify one barrier, an authorized improvement and what evidence would show the change helped.

move.control: You can make information and support clearer, discuss workload and ask responsible offices about formal requirements.
move.failure: An open invitation is used as proof of fair access while practical barriers remain.
move.next: Review one opportunity path with a colleague before the next invitation is issued.

lessons.title: Respond to concerns with credible follow-through
lessons.summary: Separate practical support, process improvement and formal workplace responsibilities.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a process suggestion from a concern requiring a designated route.
objectives: Distinguish a process suggestion from a concern requiring a designated route.
Write a response that names an owner and next action without promising an unsupported outcome.
Identify a retention response that could pressure an employee to remain silent.
takeaways: A response names a realistic next step.
Retention never requires silence about harm.
lessons.statement: Trying to keep an employee should not become a reason to minimize or privately contain a workplace concern.

image.caption: Credible follow-through includes the right route and clear responsibility.

intro.heading: Take the concern seriously without promising a conclusion
intro.body:
A leader may feel pressure to retain an employee and respond quickly with reassurance. “We will fix everything if you stay” can sound caring, but it promises an outcome the leader may not control. Another response, “let us keep this within the team,” may prevent a formal concern from reaching the responsible office. Retention work should make the workplace more credible, not create pressure to accept an informal arrangement instead of a proper process.

Listen to the actual concern and distinguish its parts. A confusing project invitation may be a process issue the supervisor can clarify. A requested accommodation needs its responsible agency route. Allegations of discrimination, harassment, retaliation or other misconduct need current formal guidance and applicable duties. The respectful-workplace policy also distinguishes its scope from protected-class and sexual-harassment policies. Do not place every concern under one convenient label.

Explain what you can do now, who must handle another part and how the employee can obtain appropriate support. Avoid making a legal finding or conducting an improvised investigation in a learning exercise. Do not promise complete confidentiality; explain the approved handling process and seek responsible advice when needed. Real concern records belong in approved channels, not course notes or a broad retention spreadsheet.

A useful response can be modest: “I can correct the unclear invitation today. I will also explain the designated route for the concern you raised and follow the responsibilities that apply to my role.” This provides action without making continued employment a condition. An employee may choose to leave while a concern still requires appropriate handling.

Follow through on the part you own. If the proposed change needs authority, identify the role and confirm the next step. Keep the employee informed as appropriate without disclosing another person’s confidential information. The goal is credible action and fair process, not a promise that every person will stay or feel satisfied.

Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Follow current agency complaint and investigation procedures; a retention conversation or informal learning plan does not postpone that responsibility.

lessons.keyStatement: A retention conversation cannot replace the responsible handling of a formal workplace concern.

items.title: “Stay and we will make it right”
items.body: Support and appropriate process should not depend on a promise to remain. State the next action within your authority and explain the responsible route for other issues. A leader can improve conditions and respond to concerns without guaranteeing a result or making the employee bargain for fair treatment.

items.title: “Let us handle it privately”
items.body: An informal discussion may be appropriate for some issues, but it cannot erase formal rights or a leader’s duties. Explain the relevant process and seek responsible guidance. Do not require direct confrontation or mediation before a route that does not require it.

items.title: “That policy covers everything”
items.body: Different kinds of concerns can fall under different policies and procedures. Check current scope through HR or the responsible office rather than giving an improvised determination. A course can teach the distinction without claiming to adjudicate an allegation or supply an agency-specific investigation plan.

tabs.label: Immediate action
tabs.body: An immediate practical action addresses what the supervisor actually controls, such as clarifying a confusing invitation. State the reason and next step without making support conditional on staying or silence. This can improve the arrangement while a separate formal concern proceeds. Do not use a small repair to imply that a larger allegation has been resolved.

tabs.label: Responsible route
tabs.body: The responsible route preserves the duties attached to a concern. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. A retention conversation does not postpone that duty. Follow current agency procedures, protect information and do not conduct an improvised course-based investigation.

tabs.label: Follow-through
tabs.body: Follow-through confirms that the owned action and required referrals actually occurred. Communicate the appropriate next information without revealing another person’s private records or promising a finding. An employee’s departure does not automatically close a concern. A credible response follows the actual responsibility and evidence, rather than measuring success only by whether the employee remains.

check.question: An employee raises a possible discrimination concern during a retention conversation. What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Explain and follow the responsible formal route while addressing any appropriate practical issue within the supervisor’s authority.
wrong: Ask the employee to promise to stay before providing support.
Keep the concern off the record to protect the retention initiative.
Decide the allegation through a course reflection exercise.
check.feedbackCorrect: This preserves formal processes and practical support without making retention the condition for a response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Fair support cannot depend on a promise to stay. Keeping an allegation off the record may suppress formal duties rather than protect the initiative. A course reflection cannot determine discrimination. Follow the current responsible process, including immediate manager reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination under Policy 1436, and address appropriate practical issues within authority.

sorting.heading: Match the response to its purpose

items.text: Clarify the published route for expressing interest in a project.
Explain the agency process for an accommodation request.
Offer support only if the employee promises not to leave.
Correct a broken link in the development invitation.
Seek current HR guidance for a reported workplace allegation.
Ask the employee to keep a possible policy concern quiet for retention statistics.

lessons.next: Next, measure whether changes improve experience and access.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Priya tells supervisor Noel that a recurring comment and uneven project access affect her experience. Noel wants to keep her and offers a project if she agrees not to report the comment. The formal concern and the project process are different issues.
options: Follow the responsible route for the concern, review project access fairly and offer support without a promise to remain silent or stay.
Keep the arrangement because it may prevent a departure.
Declare that the comment is harmless without seeking appropriate guidance.
responses: This separates issues, preserves fair access and prevents retention from becoming pressure.
A lower departure count would not justify suppressing a concern or using an inappropriate bargain.
The supervisor should not replace the relevant process with an unsupported conclusion.

lessons.transfer: Draft a practice response that separates a practical process change, a formal concern route and a realistic follow-through statement.

move.control: You can listen, explain responsible routes, make authorized changes and follow the duties of your role.
move.failure: A retention initiative becomes a private bargain that weakens access to a fair process.
move.next: Review the concern routes in your retention conversation plan with the responsible office.

lessons.title: Measure improvement without turning people into a score
lessons.summary: Use comparable process and outcome evidence, privacy protection and honest limits.
lessons.objective: Select a process measure and an outcome measure for a retention improvement.
objectives: Select a process measure and an outcome measure for a retention improvement.
Identify a comparison that cannot support a causal claim.
Describe missing or small-group information without treating it as reassurance.
takeaways: Measure the arrangement as well as departures.
lessons.statement: A lower departure count is not proof that every employee’s experience improved.

image.caption: Useful measures connect a specific change with evidence and limitations.

intro.heading: Check the effect of the arrangement
intro.body:
A retention initiative can be judged by a single figure: how many people left. That figure matters, but it cannot show whether the workplace became more understandable, respectful or usable. People may remain because they lack alternatives, and people may leave after a positive experience for another opportunity. Measure the arrangement you changed as well as relevant outcomes, using approved data and a clearly stated period.

If the change concerns project access, a process measure might examine whether invitations included criteria and an interest route before selection. Another could examine whether approved workload support was discussed. An outcome question might ask whether employees could understand and use the opportunity. These are different from a departure rate, and their definitions should match their purposes. Do not collect more personal data simply because a chart could display it.

Compare like with like. A before-and-after period may include changes in staffing, workload or role mix. A small improvement in a rate does not establish that one initiative caused it. Describe the timing and possible alternative explanations. Ask the responsible data role about appropriate comparisons and privacy handling before examining differences across groups.

Protect small or recognizable populations. Removing names from a table may still expose people when roles or events are distinctive. Use current responsible guidance rather than inventing a reporting threshold. If information cannot be reported, say that the available evidence is limited; do not display an empty chart as “no concerns.” Absence of complaints or survey responses is also not proof of a healthy climate.

Avoid scores that label an employee’s culture, commitment or intercultural orientation. This course supports analysis of arrangements and appropriately interpreted workforce evidence, not hidden personnel profiling. A useful report names the question, definitions, result, uncertainty and next decision. That makes it possible to learn without claiming more than the evidence shows.

lessons.keyStatement: Measure the process you changed and report what the evidence cannot establish.

items.title: Departures decline after a change
items.body: The timing is relevant but does not establish causation. Examine staffing, job mix, external opportunities and the length of observation. Keep the result in the report while explaining alternative interpretations. A qualified finding can still inform a practical decision without becoming a claim of proven impact.

items.title: A small subgroup has no reportable result
items.body: Privacy protection or inadequate information limits the available evidence. Do not interpret the missing cell as success, failure or absence of need. State the limitation and consider an appropriate process check that does not expose individuals. Seek responsible guidance before collecting additional sensitive information.

items.title: A participation score becomes a personnel label
items.body: Voluntary learning activity and survey participation do not establish an employee’s commitment or developmental orientation. Do not attach an inferred cultural label to a person or make the score an access gate. Analyze the work arrangement and use formal employment evidence through approved processes.

tabs.label: Definition
tabs.body: A definition states the event, population and period being measured. Departures, turnover rates and experience responses describe different things. Pair an outcome figure with a process question, such as whether employees could use the development route. This helps a leader examine the intended improvement rather than treating any lower count as proof that barriers were eliminated.

tabs.label: Limit
tabs.body: A limit explains missing information, small populations and changes in staffing or role mix. Several events may occur alongside an initiative, so a decline does not establish that the invitation alone caused it. Keep uncertainty visible and obtain appropriate data advice. Survey nonresponse is missing information, not a favorable result or an employee commitment score.

tabs.label: Decision
tabs.body: A decision uses evidence to continue, revise or investigate an arrangement. An observed improvement can justify a further check without supporting a universal success claim. Explain what the process evidence suggests and what remains unknown. Automatically discarding the figure loses information; declaring a sole cause assigns certainty the review has not earned.

check.question: A unit’s departure count falls after a new development invitation, but staffing and role mix also changed. What should the report say?
check.correct: Describe the decline and changed context, examine the opportunity process and avoid claiming that the invitation alone caused the result.
wrong: The initiative proves the unit eliminated retention barriers.
The figure is meaningless and should always be discarded.
Employees who did not answer the survey should be assigned a low commitment score.
check.feedbackCorrect: This retains the useful observation while explaining what it cannot establish and connecting it to process evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Lower departures after an invitation do not prove all retention barriers were removed. Automatically discarding the figure also loses a useful observation. Assigning commitment scores to survey nonrespondents invents personal meaning from missing data. Describe the pattern and changed context, examine process evidence and keep the causal uncertainty explicit.

items.text: The departure count declined, while staffing and role mix also changed.
One quarter proves all retention barriers disappeared.
The subgroup result cannot be reported under responsible privacy guidance.
Invitations now state criteria before the decision; access experience still needs review.
No complaints proves every employee feels included.
The survey response count is too limited to support the proposed comparison.

lessons.next: Next, build a retention improvement plan with shared responsibility.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Analyst Evan reports a lower departure count after a revised project invitation. The unit also gained several new roles, and a small group’s survey result cannot be reported. Director Lin wants to announce that the intervention solved the problem.
options: Announce success and fill the missing survey cell with a positive symbol.
Report the observed changes, process evidence and limits, then name the next question rather than asserting a solved cause.
Delete every measure because perfect evidence is unavailable.
responses: This treats uncertainty as reassurance and overstates the causal conclusion.
This keeps relevant evidence usable while making its limits and next decision explicit.
Imperfect evidence can still be useful when definitions and limitations are clear.

lessons.transfer: Create a practice report with one process measure, one outcome question, a stated period, a privacy limitation and a next decision. Label every causal claim you cannot support.

move.control: You can choose a clear question, use approved information and report limits before asking for a decision.
move.failure: A dashboard celebrates a change while missing information or alternative explanations are concealed.
move.next: Add a definitions-and-limits paragraph to the next workforce improvement report.

lessons.title: Develop a practical retention improvement plan
lessons.summary: Connect evidence to a manageable workplace change and an accountable review.
lessons.objective: Choose a retention-related change supported by the available evidence.
objectives: Choose a retention-related change supported by the available evidence.
Assign roles for implementation, formal authority and review.
Write a result statement that does not guarantee staying or equal outcomes.
takeaways: Choose a specific arrangement to improve.
Review the effect without guaranteeing retention.
lessons.statement: A retention plan should improve the workplace people use, not promise control over their career choices.

image.caption: A useful plan connects the identified barrier, responsible roles and result check.

intro.heading: Move from concern to a manageable change
intro.body:
A broad promise to improve retention can lead to many activities without a clear connection to the evidence. A practical plan begins with a specific workplace arrangement and the question it raises. If employees cannot discover project opportunities, the plan should address discovery and criteria. If workload makes participation difficult, a new celebration event will not resolve that barrier. The chosen action should have a reason another person can examine.

State the known evidence and limits in a few sentences. Describe the process gap without exposing private accounts or declaring an unsupported cause. Identify the desired result in terms of usable opportunity, clear expectations or appropriate support. “Employees can find the interest route and understand the criteria before selection” is an actionable result. “No one will ever leave” is not.

Name roles rather than assigning everything to the equity consultant. The supervisor or process owner carries out the work. HR, equal-opportunity offices or other responsible roles handle formal authority and applicable requirements. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant provides leadership, guidance, knowledge and feedback to build staff capability. Optional guidance should strengthen the staff’s work, not become a mandatory approval gate for every improvement.

Set a review at a relevant point in the work. If the change concerns the next project invitation, check the invitation before it is issued and the experience after participants use it. Keep the plan proportionate. Use approved information, current privacy guidance and responsible record practices; do not invent a retention period or put sensitive personnel details in a course artifact.

Review both progress and unintended effects. Has the process become clearer but more burdensome? Did a new interest form create an unnecessary gate? Does an employee still lack an appropriate route for a formal concern? A plan can be revised without treating the original effort as a failure. The purpose is a credible improvement process that learns over time while respecting individual career choices.

lessons.keyStatement: The plan connects a workplace barrier, an authorized change, a responsible owner and evidence of its use.

items.title: An attractive activity without a barrier link
items.body: An event may be worthwhile, but do not call it a retention intervention without explaining the question it addresses. Connect the proposed activity to evidence and a usable result. If the link is weak, revise the action rather than adding a confident outcome claim to the report.

items.title: Every action assigned to the consultant
items.body: Consultant guidance supports learning and thoughtful analysis; it does not replace a supervisor’s responsibility or HR authority. Name who operates the process and who must approve a formal change. Staff build capability by carrying out their own work with appropriate support and feedback.

items.title: A plan that promises equal outcomes
items.body: Fair and accessible processes matter, but people have different priorities and external choices. State the result within the process owner’s influence and examine differences responsibly. Do not guarantee that every employee will participate, remain or receive the same career outcome.

tabs.label: Reason
tabs.body: The reason connects an improvement to a specific observed barrier. If employees could not find the project-interest route before selection, making that route clear responds to the evidence. Explain the uncertainty and boundaries. The action is a reasonable process change, not a promise that every employee will remain or that one practice explains all departures.

tabs.label: Responsibility
tabs.body: Responsibility distinguishes who does the work, who authorizes a change and who offers guidance. The consultant can help a supervisor examine evidence and improve reasoning; the supervisor still owns the applicable workplace action. Clear roles prevent either abandoned tasks or dependency on the consultant to perform every team’s retention review.

tabs.label: Review
tabs.body: Review checks whether the changed arrangement became usable and whether it introduced new burdens. For example, verify that employees can express interest before decisions, then consider appropriate experience evidence. Keep formal concerns in their own route. A voluntary survey can inform improvement, but it cannot replace complaint handling or decide an individual employment matter.

check.question: Which result belongs in a practical retention improvement plan?
check.correct: Employees can understand and use the project-interest route before selection, with the effect reviewed through approved evidence.
wrong: Every employee from a named group will remain for a guaranteed period.
The consultant will personally perform every supervisor’s process review.
All workplace concerns will be resolved through the voluntary retention survey.
check.feedbackCorrect: This names a usable result within the process owner’s influence and an appropriate review.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A plan cannot guarantee another person’s career choice. The consultant’s guidance does not transfer every supervisor’s process responsibility. A voluntary survey cannot resolve formal complaints or employment questions. Name a usable workplace result, its responsible owner and an appropriate evidence check, while preserving any required formal route.

items.text: The invitation lacked a clear interest route; the revision makes it visible before selection.
The supervisor implements the revised invitation with required HR guidance.
No employee will leave after the new event.
The review checks whether the route was understandable and usable.
The consultant offers feedback while the process owner carries out the work.
Participation guarantees promotion and long-term retention.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to connect listening, process evidence and practical follow-through.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Celia receives comments about unclear development invitations and limited workload support. Her draft plan assigns the consultant to run every project and promises zero departures. The unit’s supervisors control invitations, and formal assignment changes need HR guidance.
options: Keep the promises because ambitious language motivates people.
Replace the evidence with a broad celebration schedule.
Assign supervisors to improve the invitation and support arrangements, involve responsible authority, seek consultant feedback and review usability without guaranteeing departures.
responses: Ambition does not make an unsupported promise or unclear responsibility workable.
A celebration schedule may not address the reported process barriers.
This connects the evidence to responsible action, appropriate support and an honest result check.

lessons.transfer: Complete a practice one-page retention improvement plan with evidence, limits, desired process result, action owner, authority route, consultant support and review.

move.control: You can improve arrangements within your authority and obtain responsible guidance for formal changes.
move.failure: A plan assigns work to the wrong role and promises an outcome no leader controls.
move.next: Choose one retention-related process question and develop a proportionate change with a named review owner.

jobAid.subtitle: From a workforce question to a credible workplace improvement.
remember: A group pattern does not explain an individual.
Listening and process evidence inform action; formal concerns retain their routes.
Retention results need definitions, privacy protection and honest limits.

sections.heading: Define
items: Name the population, period and departure boundary.
Separate representation, movement and experience questions.
Confirm appropriate references and privacy handling with responsible roles.

sections.heading: Listen and examine
items: Ask about concrete arrangements without presumed group motives.
Explain use, choice and limits of privacy.
Map discovery, criteria, workload, support and follow-through for opportunities.
Preserve designated routes for formal workplace concerns.

sections.heading: Act
items: Choose a change supported by the identified process barrier.
Name the process owner and any authority required for formal changes.
Use consultant guidance to build staff capability rather than transfer responsibility.

sections.heading: Review
items: Use comparable process and outcome evidence.
Treat missing or unreportable information as a limitation, not reassurance.
Avoid personal cultural or commitment labels.
Check unintended burdens and decide what to continue or revise.
